title: The unhired regular drummer while Jo Jones came in late
summary: Jo Jones arrived late each night so Leeman held the drum chair at the start of the evening, until he felt he could never play like Jo and Basie insisted he keep going.

story.theme_name: Playing with Count Basie: joining, leading, leaving
story.community_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people

blocks.x: Jo Jones, you asked me about -- Jo Jones always played at home with his family, he was very happy; he had children, or that was the story -- and he always used to come in an hour and a half to two hours late nights while I was in town, which was for two or three weeks, and he would depend upon Basie -- this is before the first show -- he would depend on me being in there, being on a panic and
this was probably guitarist Claude 'Fiddler' Williams; Green joined in 1937 in New York.
and still having no money to go anywhere -- that I would be there at the beginning of the evening, so I was the unhired regular drummer in the band until Jo got there, whatever time that might be.

So at his disposal, I would be there playing, and so that's the extent -- I'd either play brushes, or ... and Basie insisted that I play. I didn't want to get on that stand, and I had written my father asking if I could go back and go in with him on his trucking business, I was disillusioned that I would ever be able to play like Jo Jones. I shall never repeat this again, so you've got it on tape.

Basie forced me to go up on the stand and keep brushes, and he'd smile and he'd play and play -- at that time, I didn't know any of those things; Basie played little piano solos then, you know. I think Buster Smith made arrangements of some of those things, so he'd play -- another one was "Maple Street Rag" -- I remember they had it featuring Basie with this band background.
The saxophone player you were trying to remember was Hershel Evans.
